source.text: Karaṇīyametta Sutta (Sn 1.8), Sutta Nipāta, Khuddaka Nikāya of the Pāli Canon: all 10 verses
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

mt01.heading: Verse 1 · What Should Be Done
mt01.plain: This is what should be done by one skilled in what is good, who wishes to reach the state of peace: be capable, upright, truly straight, easy to speak to, gentle and not proud.
mt01.commentary: It is said that when monks practicing in the forest were troubled by tree spirits, the Buddha taught them this discourse and sent them back with loving-kindness. Before cultivating loving-kindness, it first says what kind of person one should be.

mt02.heading: Verse 2 · A Simple Life
mt02.plain: Contented and easy to support, with few duties and a light way of living, with calm senses and prudent, not impudent, and not greedily clinging to families.
mt02.commentary: A simple life of few possessions and few wants is the ground of loving-kindness. With many desires it is hard to embrace others generously.

mt03.heading: Verse 3 · May All Beings Be Happy
mt03.plain: Do not do even the slightest thing that the wise would rebuke. May all beings be happy and safe. May all beings be happy at heart.
mt03.commentary: Here the wishes of loving-kindness begin. "Sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā" (may all beings be happy) is the line most often repeated in loving-kindness meditation.

mt04.heading: Verse 4 · All Life, Great and Small
mt04.plain: Whatever living beings there may be, weak or strong, without exception, long or large, medium or short, small or gross,
mt04.commentary: The circle of those who receive loving-kindness widens one by one. It does not choose between strong and weak, large and small.

mt05.heading: Verse 5 · Seen or Unseen
mt05.plain: seen or unseen, living far or near, already born or seeking birth: may all beings be happy at heart.
mt05.commentary: Loving-kindness reaches even unseen beings, distant beings and beings not yet born. Loving-kindness has no boundaries.

mt06.heading: Verse 6 · May They Not Harm One Another
mt06.plain: Let no one deceive another or despise anyone anywhere. In anger or ill will, let no one wish suffering on another.
mt06.commentary: Loving-kindness does not stop at wishing others happiness; it goes on to lay down deceit, contempt and hatred.

mt07.heading: Verse 7 · Like a Mother Guarding Her Only Child
mt07.plain: Just as a mother would guard her only child with her own life, so toward all living beings one should cultivate a boundless heart.
mt07.commentary: The most beautiful image in the discourse. It asks us to give every living being the same heart as a mother who would give her life to protect her only child.

mt08.heading: Verse 8 · Loving-Kindness for the Whole World
mt08.plain: Toward the whole world one should cultivate a boundless heart of loving-kindness: above, below and all around, unobstructed, without hatred, without enmity.
mt08.commentary: Loving-kindness spreads unobstructed in every direction. A heart without hatred or enemies is itself the greatest protection.

mt09.heading: Verse 9 · The Sublime Abiding
mt09.plain: Standing or walking, sitting or lying down, as long as one is awake, one should hold firmly to this mindfulness. This, they say, is the sublime abiding here.
mt09.commentary: Loving-kindness is not only for meditation time but a heart held in every waking moment, walking, standing, sitting and lying down. The "sublime abiding" refers to the four immeasurables: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity.

mt10.heading: Verse 10 · Not Born Again
mt10.plain: Not falling into wrong views, virtuous and endowed with right insight, having overcome greed for sensual desires, one never again lies in a womb.
mt10.commentary: The discourse ends by saying the path of loving-kindness finally leads to liberation. It shows that warmth toward others and right insight into oneself must go together.

metta.definition: Mettā: a warm heart that wishes all beings to be happy. It comes from the word for friend (mitta). The first of the four immeasurables.

brahmavihara.definition: Brahmavihāra: abiding in the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity.
